lesson.title: Three by three: the determinant and the cross product

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the unit cube's box keeping its volume, the determinant, as k's tip slides sideways, then going flat at 0 as k drops to the floor, when you drag where k lands.
interactive.title: The unit cube and its box
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Thirteen small screens share one picture. Most show a 3-D view of the unit cube. The arrows i, j and k run along three of its edges, each named beside its tip. i points across, j points along and k points up. Every point is written (across, along, up). You can drag the background to turn the view. The matrix reads out beside the view. A readout shows the box's volume, which is the determinant.

The rule. A 3 by 3 matrix sends i, j and k to its three columns. The unit cube goes with them and leans into a slanted box. If i and j stay on the floor, the floor stays the unit square, with area 1. Then the box's volume is its height. That height is k's up part. In general, the determinant comes from the top row. Cover an entry's row and column. The 2 by 2 left over gives its minor, ad − bc. Give the three minors the signs +, −, +. Then multiply each top-row entry by its signed minor and add the three.

The screens.
- 1, the box. k's tip slides from (0, 0, 1) to (1, 0.5, 2). The cube leans into a box. The matrix's third column changes to (1, 0.5, 2). This plays once as the screen opens. Its still shows the leaning box, read as: a 3 by 3 matrix moves every point of space. Its columns are where i, j and k land. Here i and j stay on the floor, and k lands on (1, 0.5, 2). The unit cube leans into a slanted box.
- 2, a puzzle. The matrix [2 1 0; 0 3 1; 0 0 2] moves space. Where does j land? The answers are (1, 3, 0), (0, 3, 1) and (2, 0, 0). Picking (0, 3, 1) gets the hint: that is row 2. Where j lands is read down column 2. Picking (2, 0, 0) gets the hint: that is column 1, where i lands. After Check, i, j and k swing to the three columns. j lands on (1, 3, 0).
- 3, the volume. k's tip is back on (1, 0.5, 2). The readout shows floor 1 × height 2 = volume 2. k's tip slides sideways to (−1, 1, 2). The box leans the other way, and the volume stays 2. This plays once as the screen opens. Then k's tip is yours to drag. Dragging moves it across and up. Its along part stays put, and the readouts follow. Its still shows the box leaning back, read as: the floor is still the unit square. So the box's volume is its height, k's up part, 2. That volume is the determinant. It is the factor the move scales every volume by. Sliding k's tip sideways leans the box but keeps its height. So the volume stays 2.
- 4, a puzzle. i and j stay on the floor, and k lands on (2, −1, 3). What is the determinant? The answers are 3, 6 and 4. Picking 6 gets the hint: only the up part sets the height. The 2 across just leans the box. Picking 4 gets the hint: the volume is not k's parts added up. It is the floor's area times the height. After Check, k's tip moves to (2, −1, 3), and the volume reads 3.
- 5, flat. k's tip drops straight down from (1, 0.5, 2) to (1, 0.5, 0). The box gets lower. The volume reads 2, then 1, then 0. On the floor the box is flat. This plays once as the screen opens. Then k's tip is yours to drag. Below the floor the box comes out mirrored, and the volume reads negative. Its still shows the flat box, read as: as k's tip drops, the box gets lower and its volume falls. On the floor the box is flat, and the determinant is 0. All of space lands on that one flat plane. So the move cannot be undone. Push k's tip below the floor and the box comes out mirrored, with a negative volume.
- 6, a puzzle. i and j stay on the floor. Which landing spot for k squashes space flat? The answers are (3, 2, 0), (0, 0, 3) and (1, 1, 1). Picking (0, 0, 3) gets the hint: that stands straight up 3, so the box's volume is 3. Picking (1, 1, 1) gets the hint: its up part is 1, so the box has volume 1. After Check, the box flattens onto the floor, and the volume reads 0.
- 7, the recipe. Now i lands on (2, 1, 0), j on (1, 3, 0) and k on (1, 0, 2). The matrix is [2 1 1; 1 3 0; 0 0 2]. The floor is a parallelogram, and the box rises from it. The working lights each top-row entry in turn. It greys out that entry's row and column. The first entry, 2, leaves [3 0; 0 2]. Its minor is 6. The second, 1, leaves [1 0; 0 2]. Its minor is 2, and it takes a minus. The third, 1, leaves [1 3; 0 0]. Its minor is 0. The total is 2 × 6 − 1 × 2 + 1 × 0 = 10. Beside it, floor 5 × height 2 = 10. The floor's area is 2 × 3 − 1 × 1 = 5. This plays once as the screen opens. Its still shows the finished working beside the box, read as: take each top-row entry in turn. Cover its row and column. The 2 by 2 left gives its minor, its ad − bc. With the signs + − +, the minors become cofactors. Multiply each entry by its cofactor and add them up. That gives 2 × 6 − 1 × 2 + 1 × 0 = 10. The box agrees. Its floor is the parallelogram of i and j, with area 2 × 3 − 1 × 1 = 5. Floor 5 times height 2 is 10.
- 8, a puzzle. What is the determinant of [3 1 0; 1 2 1; 0 1 2]? The answers are 7, 11 and 12. Picking 11 gets the hint: the middle term takes a minus. The signs go + − +. Picking 12 gets the hint: that multiplies down the diagonal only. Each top-row entry needs its own minor. After Check, the working fills in: 3 × 3 − 1 × 2 + 0 × 1 = 7. The box of its three columns shows volume 7.
- 9, the cross product. The floor of screen 7 comes back alone. It is the parallelogram of a = (2, 1, 0) and b = (1, 3, 0). The grid [i j k; 2 1 0; 1 3 0] reads out beside it. The working runs the same recipe: i(1 × 0 − 0 × 3) − j(2 × 0 − 0 × 1) + k(2 × 3 − 1 × 1) = 5k. Then an arrow a × b grows straight up from the floor to length 5. This plays once as the screen opens. Its still shows the arrow standing on the floor, read as: put i, j and k in the top row as if they were numbers. Put a in row 2 and b in row 3. The same recipe gives a × b. Here it is 5k. Its dot product with a and with b is 0, so it stands square to both. Its length, 5, is the floor's area.
- 10, a puzzle. What does the recipe give for j × i? Row 2 is j = (0, 1, 0), and row 3 is i = (1, 0, 0). The answers are −k, k and 0. Picking k gets the hint: that is i × j. Here the rows are swapped, so the sign flips. Picking 0 gets the hint: i and j make a floor of area 1, so the arrow has length 1. After Check, the working shows the k part 0 × 0 − 1 × 1 = −1. The arrow points down from the floor.
- 11, the circuit. Three loops sit in a row. Each end loop has 3 Ω of its own. The middle loop has 6 Ω of its own. Each pair of neighbours shares a 3 Ω resistor. The loop currents I₁, I₂ and I₃ are drawn clockwise. The resistance grid [6 −3 0; −3 12 −3; 0 −3 6] reads out. The recipe runs along its top row: 6 × 63 − (−3) × (−18) + 0 × 9 = 378 − 54 = 324. This plays once as the screen opens. Its still shows the circuit and the finished working, read as: a three-loop circuit's resistance grid is [6 −3 0; −3 12 −3; 0 −3 6]. Each diagonal entry is a loop's total resistance. Each shared 3 Ω becomes −3. The top-row recipe gives 6 × 63 − (−3) × (−18) + 0 × 9 = 324. It is not zero, so the grid does not squash space flat. That means exactly one set of loop currents fits, whatever the loop voltages.
- 12, a mixed puzzle. A spanner lies along r = (0.3, 0, 0) m. You push with F = (80, 150, 0) N. What is the moment, r × F? The answers are 45 N m along k, 51 N m along k and 45 N m along −k. Picking 51 N m gets the hint: that uses the whole 170 N push. The 80 N along the handle turns nothing, and the recipe drops it. Picking 45 N m along −k gets the hint: that is F × r. Put r in row 2 and F in row 3. After Check, the working shows 0.3 × 150 − 0 × 80 = 45 for the k part. The moment arrow stands along the bolt.
- 13, a mixed puzzle. What is the determinant of [1 2 3; 4 5 6; 7 8 9]? The answers are 0, −24 and 45. Picking −24 gets the hint: the middle term takes a minus, so −2 × (−6) is +12. Picking 45 gets the hint: that multiplies down the diagonal only. After Check, the working shows 1 × (−3) − 2 × (−6) + 3 × (−3) = 0. The box of its columns flattens. Column 2 sits halfway between columns 1 and 3, so all three lie in one flat plane.

Some screens show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. On a narrow phone they wrap onto more lines, and no word splits. A wrong pick is drawn, so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The 3-D view is drawn on a flat screen, so some lengths look shorter than they are. The readouts give the true values. The picture shows three arrows and one box. The move acts on every point of space, though. The circuit is ideal, with fixed resistances and no wire resistance. Its values are example figures. The top-row recipe works for bigger grids too. It soon gets long, though.

explain.text:
A 3 by 3 matrix moves all of space at once. Its three columns are where the arrows i, j and k land. Its determinant does for volumes what ad − bc did for areas. You find it from the top row. Multiply each entry by a signed 2 by 2 determinant, then add them all up. With i, j and k in the top row, the same recipe gives the cross product.

Start from the unit cube, with edges i, j and k. Its volume is 1. Keep i and j where they are, and move only k. Then the floor stays the unit square. The cube leans into a slanted box. A box's volume is its floor's area times its height. The floor's area is 1, so the volume is the height. That height is k's up part. Slide k's tip sideways and the box leans, but its height stays the same. So the volume stays the same too. That is the shear you met in the plane, one size up. The same holds for every 3 by 3 matrix. Its determinant's size is the factor it scales every volume by. Drop k's tip to the floor and the box is flat. So the determinant is 0. All of space then lies on one plane, and no move can lift it back. Push the tip below the floor and the box comes out mirrored. A move that flips space like that has a negative determinant.[^1]

Here is the recipe for any 3 by 3 grid. Take a top-row entry and cover its row and its column. A 2 by 2 grid is left. Its ad − bc is that entry's [[minor]]. Do the same for the other two entries. Give the three minors the signs +, −, +, and they become [[cofactor]]s. Multiply each top-row entry by its cofactor and add the three.[^2] Try it on a box whose floor is not square. Send i to (2, 1, 0), j to (1, 3, 0) and k to (1, 0, 2). The top row is 2, 1, 1, and the minors are 6, 2 and 0. So the determinant is 2 × 6 − 1 × 2 + 1 × 0 = 10. Now check it as a box. The floor is the parallelogram of i and j. Its area is 2 × 3 − 1 × 1 = 5. The height is 2. So the volume is 5 × 2 = 10, and the two agree. Forget the middle minus and you get 14, which fails the check.

The cross product comes from the same recipe. Put i, j and k in the top row as if they were numbers. Put a in row 2 and b in row 3.[^3] Here a and b sit in rows, not columns. That is fine. Turning a grid's rows into columns leaves its determinant the same, so either way works. The three cofactors are then a × b's i, j and k parts. Take a = (2, 1, 0) and b = (1, 3, 0), the floor above. The i and j parts come out 0. The k part is 2 × 3 − 1 × 1 = 5. So a × b = 5k. It stands square to the floor, and its length is the floor's area. That is also why the recipe works for any grid. The top row's three cofactors are the parts of row 2 × row 3. That arrow stands square to the floor those two rows make. Its length is that floor's area. So its dot product with row 1 is the floor's area times row 1's height above it. That is the volume of the box the three rows make. Swap rows 2 and 3 and every part changes sign, so b × a = −5k. To check the order, try i × j. It must give k.

Three-phase work uses a 3 by 3 matrix too. Its symmetrical components split an unbalanced set of three phasors into three balanced sets.[^4] That matrix holds complex numbers, so it waits for later.

**A 3 by 3 determinant is the volume scale factor. It is 0 when space is squashed flat. To find it, go along the top row: each entry times its cofactor, with signs + − +, added up. With i, j and k in the top row, the same recipe gives a × b.**

analogy.text: Think of a transformer core's stack of steel laminations, squared up on the bench. Push the top so the stack leans. Each sheet slides a little over the one below. The stack now leans, but its floor and its height are unchanged. So it holds the same steel. That is k's tip sliding sideways. With the floor fixed, the box's volume changes only when its height does.
analogy.breaks: Laminations are separate sheets that slide in steps. A matrix leans all of space smoothly. Real steel barely changes its volume. A matrix can stretch volumes, flip them or squash them to 0.

practice.text:
- Write where i, j and k land as the grid's three columns. For a cross product, put i, j and k in the top row. Put a under them, and b under a.
- Take the top-row entries one at a time. Cover that entry's row and column.
- Work out ad − bc for the 2 by 2 left over. That is its minor.
- Give the three minors the signs +, −, +.
- Multiply each top-row entry by its signed minor, and add the three.
- Check a cross product's order on i × j. It must give k.

**Rules of thumb:** A zero in the top row saves work, because its term drops out. A determinant of 0 means space is squashed onto a plane, a line or a point. Then the move cannot be undone. Swap two rows and the sign flips.

**Worked example:** Three loops sit in a row. Each end loop has 3 Ω of its own. The middle loop has 6 Ω of its own. Each pair of neighbours shares a 3 Ω resistor. These are example figures. With all three loop currents drawn clockwise, the resistance grid is [6 −3 0; −3 12 −3; 0 −3 6]. Cover row 1 and column 1. What is left gives 12 × 6 − (−3) × (−3) = 72 − 9 = 63. Cover row 1 and column 2. What is left gives (−3) × 6 − (−3) × 0 = −18. The third top-row entry is 0, so its term drops out. The determinant is 6 × 63 − (−3) × (−18) + 0 = 378 − 54 = 324. It is not zero, so exactly one set of loop currents fits.

**Common mistakes**
- Forgetting the minus on the middle term. In the worked example that gives 432.
- Multiplying down the diagonal only.
- Covering the wrong row or column. Cover the entry's own row and its own column.
- Reading where an arrow lands along a row. It is read down a column.
- Putting b above a in a cross product. That flips the answer's sign.

interactive.html:
Most screens show a 3-D view of the unit cube, and the slanted box a 3 by 3 matrix makes of it.

The determinant is the box's volume. The top-row recipe finds it, and gives the cross product.
interactive.title: The unit cube and its box
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the unit cube's box keeping its volume, the determinant, as k's tip slides sideways, then going flat at 0 as k drops to the floor, when you drag where k lands.

checks.label: A three by three determinant is obtained by multiplying each element of the first row by its corresponding cofactor and then adding the three together: on each screen that works one out, the minors and the total drawn are that sum, it agrees with the full six-term formula, and the box drawn has that volume

Any transformation that inverts the orientation of space has a negative determinant: with k's tip pushed below the floor the box comes out mirrored and its volume reads negative, and lifted back above the floor it reads positive again

The cross product is really the determinant of a grid with i, j and k in its top row: on each cross product screen the cofactors are the parts of the arrow drawn, they match the part by part formula, and the arrow stands square to both rows
With i and j on the floor the volume is the height: wherever k's tip is dragged, the volume shown is k's up part, the third column is k's tip, and sliding it sideways leaves the volume alone
Dropping k's tip to the floor squashes the box flat: the volume reads 0, every point of space lands on the floor, and the puzzle's flat pick lies on the floor too

Every worked number is right: minors 6, 2 and 0 give 10, and the box's floor 5 times height 2 agrees (14 without the minus); minors 3, 2 and 1 give 7 (11 without the minus, 12 down the diagonal); a × b = 5k and j × i = −k; the circuit's grid has 6, 12 and −3, minors 63, −18 and 9, and 378 − 54 = 324 (432 without the minus); r × F = 45k (51 from the whole 170 N); [1 2 3; 4 5 6; 7 8 9] has minors −3, −6 and −3 and gives 0 (−24 without the minus, 45 down the diagonal); k on (2, −1, 3) gives 3 (6 and 4 are slips)
Each puzzle's answer comes from the rule, and each wrong answer offered is the slip its hint names
Each puzzle offers three different answers, accepts only the right one, and draws every wrong one in the warning colour
Before Check, no puzzle shows its answer; after a right answer, it does

Each demonstration ends where the lesson says: k on (1, 0.5, 2) with volume 2, then slid to (−1, 1, 2) keeping volume 2 all the way, then dropped to the floor with volume 0; the recipe's box on [2 1 1; 1 3 0; 0 0 2] with volume 10; a × b standing at 5k
Every demonstration has finished arriving within its 3 to 4.5 s, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 2.5 s

applied.problem: A negative determinant cannot be the factor a volume is scaled by; its size is, and the sign says flipped. Also, no screen or earlier lesson showed Dan that a × b’s length is the floor’s area, so “as you found with the spanner” claims a finding he never made.
